title: Do microwaves cook food from the inside out?
hook: If they did, the middle of the plate wouldn’t stay cold.
summary: No: microwaves heat the outer layers of food, and the heat reaches the centre gradually, by conduction.

cardBlocks.text: Lots of people have heard that a microwave cooks food from the inside out. But if that were true, the middle of the plate wouldn’t stay cold while the edges scald. What actually happens is that microwaves reach only a few centimetres into food: heating is fairly even in the outer 25 to 38 millimetres of a uniform, watery food.

Further in, the heat spreads slowly by conduction, as in any other cooking. That is why many food packages ask for a "stand time" after heating: it lets the heat reach the centre until the temperature evens out.
Microwaves heat the outer layers; the centre warms later by conduction, which is why stand time helps.

deepDiveBlocks.text: In some foods the centre really does heat first. If the surface is drier than the inside, as with bread or a baked potato, or if a moist filling sits under a dry crust, the filling can end up hotter than the outside.
Microwaves make polar molecules in food, such as water, rotate as they try to line up with the electric field. That movement produces heat.

heroMedia.alt: Diagram of food cut in half: microwaves heat only the outer layers, and heat reaches the centre slowly by conduction; beside it, a water molecule spinning.

claims.text: People often hear that microwaves cook from the inside out, yet the centre of the plate is often colder than the edges.

support.excerpt: I’ve been told by everyone that “a microwave oven cooks from the inside out.” If that’s so, then why is my plate of food always coldest in the center, while the outside edges are scalding hot?
it’s not necessarily accurate to say the food is cooked from the inside out.

claims.text: Heating is fairly even in the outer 25–38 mm of a uniform, high-water food.

support.excerpt: the heating effect is fairly uniform in the outer 25–38 mm (1–1.5 inches) of a homogeneous, high-water-content food item.
most of the microwave energy will be absorbed by the water near the surface before it gets into the center of the food

claims.text: Then heat spreads through the food by conduction, as with any contact with a hotter body.

support.excerpt: Once the electrical field's energy is initially absorbed, heat will gradually spread through the object similarly to any other contact with a hotter body.

claims.text: Stand time after heating lets heat spread by conduction until the temperature is even.

support.excerpt: after you remove the food from the microwave, you’re supposed to let it stand for a prescribed time before serving. This lets the heat diffuse through the food via ordinary conduction so that a uniform temperature is reached.

claims.text: If the surface is drier than the inside, as with bread, a baked potato or a moist filling under a dry crust, the centre can heat faster.

support.excerpt: if the surface of the food is drier than the center, as with bread or a baked potato, the center will heat up faster. You can see this clearly if you microwave foods with a dry outer crust and a moist filling

claims.text: Microwaves make polar molecules in food rotate to line up with the field, which produces heat.

support.excerpt: is induces polar molecules in the food to rotate and produce thermal energy (heat) in a process known as dielectric heating.
